Hypothesis: We hypothesize that in HCC, HDAC1 upregulation specifically catalyzes histone deacetylation at targeted genomic regions, leading to a modified chromatin landscape characterized by nucleosome repositioning and diminished recruitment of DNA repair proteins. This epigenetic remodeling disrupts normal p53 and MYC regulatory interactions with DNA repair pathways, thereby establishing defined chromatin 'hotspots' that facilitate the preferential integration of hepatitis virus DNA. The accumulation of such integration events drives genomic instability, which in turn triggers oncogenic processes including aberrant autophagic responses, enhanced metastatic potential, and increased angiogenesis. We propose to test this hypothesis using CRISPR-based epigenome editing, combined with high-resolution mapping of viral integration sites and chromatin accessibility assays (e.g., ATAC-seq and ChIP-seq), and by directly comparing the functional contributions of HDAC1 versus its paralogs, HDAC2 and HDAC3.
Abstract: In hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), we propose that upregulation of HDAC1 initiates a specific cascade of epigenetic events that not only alters global transcriptional dynamics but also creates defined chromatin hotspots conducive to hepatitis viral DNA integration. Specifically, HDAC1-driven histone deacetylation reconfigures local chromatin architecture by repositioning nucleosomes and reducing the accessibility of DNA repair proteins at key genomic loci. This disruption interferes with the normal regulatory interactions of p53 and MYC with repair pathways, facilitating the persistence and accumulation of viral integration events. The ensuing genomic instability is hypothesized to underpin oncogenic processes including autophagy modulation, metastasis, and angiogenesis. To test this mechanism, we will employ CRISPR-based epigenome modulation in tandem with high-resolution integration mapping and assays of chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq and ChIP-seq), alongside comparative analyses with HDAC2 and HDAC3, thereby clarifying HDAC1’s unique role in HCC pathogenesis.
CausalChain: HDAC1 upregulation -> increased histone deacetylation -> altered chromatin landscape (nucleosome repositioning & reduced repair protein accessibility) -> modulation of p53/MYC-controlled DNA repair pathways -> formation of viral integration hotspots -> enhanced hepatitis virus DNA integration -> genomic instability -> downstream oncogenic processes (autophagic dysregulation, metastasis, angiogenesis)
